title: New Foremen Onboarding
body: Most of the Stage 4, Stage 6, and ROM pad NCRs trace back to a supervisor who was on the ground but didn't catch or act on the problem. A foreman who's never been walked through field inspection, NCR writing, and coaching under pressure is going to repeat that pattern — not because they don't care, but because nobody built the habit.
keyPoints: Readiness isn't a one-day induction — it's four weeks: foundations, technical/field competency, leadership and communication, then a supervised full shift before sign-off.
The Week 4 call is three-way: Ready, Ready with support, or Not yet ready. A "not yet" needs a real additional-training path, not a shrug and a second attempt.
Shift handover gets its own module in Week 1 because so many incidents cluster right at shift start/end — poor handover discipline is a direct line to an NCR.
Coaching under pressure is a trained skill: when a PM fires five questions at once, the right move is to stay calm and ask what can improve, not defend every point.
Language barriers on a crew are a shift-readiness issue, not a side note — if a foreman can't communicate assertively under pressure, that's a Week 3 gap, not a personality quirk.
apply: If you've got a recently promoted foreman running a face or a dump point solo, don't just check their numbers — watch how they handle the next handover or the next pushback from a driver or PM. That's the tell on whether the onboarding actually took.
